core: The working definition of the presidency: the office of the U.S. chief executive and the head of the executive branch (Article II, Section 1 vesting clause; White House framing)
The constitutional role: Article II of the Constitution creates the presidency, one factual line
The four named roles, each with one line: commander-in-chief, chief executive, chief diplomat, veto holder
Selection: the Electoral College, named with one factual line (elections mechanics belong to the sibling topic)
Powers and limits, each with one line: executive orders, pardons, appointments with Senate confirmation
The honest note: the office has grown far beyond 1787 expectations, stated factually
The honest framing: the presidency is one person with a very large desk
supporting: Constitutional qualifications: natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, 14 years a resident (Article II, Section 1)
Four-year term, with the Vice President chosen for the same term
The State of the Union duty (Article II, Section 3)
Treaty power shared with the Senate: two-thirds of Senators present must concur
Veto override: Congress may override with a two-thirds vote of both houses
Pardons cover federal offenses only and not cases of impeachment

claims.claim: Article II, Section 1 of the U.S. Constitution vests the executive power in a single office: 'The executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America.'

The presidency is the office of the U.S. chief executive and the head of the executive branch: the president is responsible for executing and enforcing the laws Congress writes, grounded in Article II, Section 3 ('he shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed').

The Constitution names the president commander-in-chief of the armed forces: Article II, Section 2 makes the president 'Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States, and of the Militia of the several States, when called into the actual Service of the United States.'

The president acts as the nation's chief diplomat: the Executive Branch conducts diplomacy with other nations, the president has the power to negotiate and sign treaties that the Senate must ratify, and Article II, Section 3 provides that the president 'shall receive Ambassadors and other public Ministers.'
The president holds the veto: the president may sign legislation into law or veto bills enacted by Congress, and Congress may override a veto with a two-thirds vote of both houses.

The president is not elected directly by popular vote: voters choose the members of the Electoral College, and those electors cast the votes for president. The National Archives describes the Electoral College as 'a Process, not a Place' — the term does not appear in the Constitution. There are 538 electors (each state gets as many electors as it has members of Congress, plus three for the District of Columbia), and a candidate needs at least 270 electoral votes to win.
The president can issue executive orders, which direct executive officers or clarify and further existing laws.
The president has the power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment (Article II, Section 2).

The president's power to staff the government is shared with the Senate: the president nominates ambassadors, Supreme Court justices, and other officers of the United States 'by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate' (Article II, Section 2).

The presidential office has grown far beyond the expectations of 1787: since its invention at the Constitutional Convention of 1787, the office has gradually become more powerful, and its occupants have far greater opportunities to exercise leadership at home and abroad than the original design anticipated.

The Constitution sets three qualifications for the presidency: the president must be a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years of age, and a resident of the United States for at least 14 years (Article II, Section 1).

The president serves a four-year term and must 'from time to time give to the Congress Information of the State of the Union' (Article II, Section 3); presidents traditionally deliver a State of the Union address to a joint session of Congress each January except in inaugural years.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the framers of 1787 designed a strong or a weak executive, and whether the office's growth since then is a departure from or a fulfillment of the design.
positions: The Articles of Confederation made no provision for an executive branch at all, and early Convention proposals ranged from a weak committee removable by state governors to Alexander Hamilton's call for a single powerful executive serving for life (OpenStax 12.1).

The office that emerged in 1787 was a single president whose most important powers — treaties and appointments — were shared with the Senate, and since 1787 the office has gradually accumulated more power (OpenStax 12.1).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both facts without adjudicating: the 1787 design created one president with shared powers, and the office has grown over time. The growth is presented as a documented historical fact (OpenStax 12.1), not as a judgment about whether that growth is good or bad.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The scope of the commander-in-chief power — whether it includes the power to initiate military action without Congress.
positions: The constitutional text names the president commander in chief of the Army and Navy, without spelling out the boundaries of that authority in wartime (Article II, Section 2).
War powers are debated in scholarship and in practice between the president and Congress.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson stays with the constitutional text and the White House description (commander-in-chief of the armed forces) and does not enter the war-powers debate, which belongs to a more advanced treatment.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Electoral College is accurately described as 'indirect election' given that the popular vote decides who each state's electors are.
positions: USA.gov: 'The president and vice president are not elected directly by citizens. Instead, they are chosen through the Electoral College process.'
The National Archives: the Electoral College is the process by which the United States elects the President, though the term does not appear in the Constitution.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the mechanism factually: voters cast ballots for president, those ballots choose each state's electors, and the electors cast the official votes. Full election mechanics belong to the sibling elections topic.
